lessons.title: From Burnash's catchment idea to this repository
lessons.summary: Understand what SAC-SMA represents, what it deliberately leaves unresolved, and where the implementation lives.

inline.text: The Sacramento Soil Moisture Accounting model: a lumped or semi-distributed conceptual rainfall-runoff accounting system whose calibrated stores and transfer rules reproduce catchment response without solving a spatial Richards equation.

Think of the model as a deterministic state machine. A state vector of water-depth stores enters a timestep; precipitation and potential evapotranspiration are inputs; the code applies ordered transfer rules; updated stores and channel-flow components leave the timestep. The 1973 Burnash, Ferral, and McGuire report is the historical formulation, while the pinned source is authoritative for this implementation.

content.title: A calibrated tank is not a literal soil layer

inline.text: Store capacities and recession parameters summarize catchment behavior. A good hydrograph fit does not prove that each internal store equals a measured soil horizon or that parameters transfer unchanged to a different climate, scale, or land cover.

content.title: Read a dry-start response
content.scenario: A dry HRU receives light rainfall smaller than its upper tension-water deficit.

steps.text: The rainfall first replenishes UZTWC because TWX remains zero.
With no upper free water, percolation and interflow do not activate.
Only minimum impervious runoff can respond immediately, proportional to PCTIM.

content.result: Most water becomes state rather than channel inflow.
content.interpretation: This is structural behavior, not a numerical accident; calibration can change thresholds but not remove the process ordering.

content.title: A wet and dry basin share one parameter set
content.observed_behavior: The dry basin is reasonable but the persistently wet basin underestimates fast runoff.
content.conditions: The same calibrated conceptual parameters were transferred across regimes.
content.candidate_causes: Forcing bias; parameter non-transferability; missing saturation-excess structure; wrong HRU representation.
content.reasoning: The model's calibrated stores are effective catchment quantities. Persistent regime-dependent error can be structural or a transfer error, not merely one bad coefficient.
content.recommended_action: Check forcing and state initialization, stratify residuals by wetness, then test separate parameterizations or a model with more explicit spatial saturation behavior.

content.title: Ordering is part of the model

inline.text: Do not refactor all ET withdrawals into an unordered vector operation unless equivalence is proved. Earlier withdrawals change the residual demand and relative saturation used by later branches.

content.title: Upper-zone ET
content.scenario: EP is 4 mm, UZTWC is 15 mm, and UZTWM is 30 mm.

steps.text: Relative fullness is 15/30 = 0.5.
E1 is 4 mm times 0.5 = 2 mm.
UZTWC becomes 13 mm and residual demand is 2 mm before later withdrawals.

content.interpretation: This is a nonlinear sequence once storage bounds, free-water transfer, and later lower-zone terms are included.

content.title: Negative storage after a port
content.observed_behavior: A C++ translation occasionally produces negative UZTWC after large PET.
content.conditions: The direct formula was ported but the Fortran clamp-and-correct branch was omitted.
content.candidate_causes: Missing bound correction; rate/depth unit mismatch; stale state reference.
content.reasoning: The source corrects E1 when subtraction crosses zero. Omitting that guard violates a state invariant and also leaves the wrong residual demand.
content.recommended_action: Port each mutation and its immediately following bounds check as one tested operation; assert every content remains within capacity.

lessons.title: How water chooses fast and slow paths
lessons.summary: Follow water as it moves along fast surface paths or enters slower stores, then connect each path to the source.

inline.text: Some ground sheds rain at once because water cannot soak through it. A roof is a simple example. Other ground starts to shed more rain only after its soil becomes wet. The model represents these two areas separately before it computes runoff.

Impervious means that water cannot readily pass through a surface. PCTIM is the permanently impervious area fraction. ADIMP joins ADditional and IMpervious; it is the extra area fraction that produces more runoff as it gets wet. ADIMC is a water-depth state, not an area. It controls wetness over ADIMP. PAREA is the remaining pervious area fraction, where pervious means that water can enter the soil.

content.title: Dry-to-wet behavior of the three area fractions
content.scenario: Use PCTIM = 0.10 and ADIMP = 0.20. Then PAREA = 1 - 0.20 - 0.10 = 0.70. Let 10 mm of rain fall and ignore every other process.

steps.text: The permanent area always sends 10 mm times 0.10 = 1.0 mm of basin-average water directly toward runoff.
When ADIMC is near its lower bound, little of the 0.20 additional area acts impervious. Most of its rain can still enter storage.
At intermediate ADIMC, part of that 0.20 area adds direct runoff. The exact amount follows the source's wetness ratio and square.
Near the ADIMC upper limit, almost all of the additional area can shed rain quickly. It can add up to 10 mm times 0.20 = 2.0 mm.

content.result: The fixed direct contribution is 1.0 mm. The wetness-dependent contribution ranges from near 0 to near 2.0 mm. The 0.70 PAREA follows the soil-store paths.
content.interpretation: PCTIM and ADIMP are area fractions. ADIMC is the changing water depth that controls ADIMP. PAREA is the remainder, so these names are not interchangeable.

content.title: Calibration cannot repair the wrong runoff mechanism

inline.text: If a catchment response is dominated by infiltration-excess physics, frozen soils, reservoir operations, or spatial connectivity absent from this formulation, tuning conceptual capacities may fit one period while producing systematic errors elsewhere.

content.title: Percolation before clamps
content.scenario: PERCM is 3 mm per substep, UZFWC/UZFWM is 0.5, DEFR is 0.8, ZPERC is 4, and REXP is 2.

steps.text: Dryness contribution is 0.8 squared = 0.64.
Multiplier is 1 + 4 times 0.64 = 3.56.
Candidate PERC is 3 times 0.5 times 3.56 = 5.34 mm.
Clamp it to available UZFWC and remaining lower-zone capacity.

content.result: 5.34 mm is a candidate, never permission to create water.
content.interpretation: The guards are integral to conservation and must survive a translation.

content.title: Flashy peaks and weak recession
content.observed_behavior: Storm peaks are too high while dry-weather flow dies too quickly.
content.conditions: Forcing timing is verified and mass balance closes.
content.candidate_causes: Excess PCTIM/ADIMP; too-fast LZPK/LZSK; deficient lower storage; structural mismatch.
content.reasoning: Closed balance rules out lost water but not wrong path allocation. Fast area fractions raise immediate runoff; recession parameters and capacities control delayed drainage.

inline.text: The BMI supplies precipitation and PET as rates in mm/s. runSac multiplies each by the driver timestep in seconds, producing depths. EXSAC converts that timestep to days because SAC1's recession coefficients are daily. SAC1 then chooses enough internal increments that UZFWC + TWX contributes no more than roughly 5 mm per increment.

content.title: Smaller driver steps are not automatically equivalent

inline.text: Adaptive substeps reduce sensitivity to large water amounts, but branch ordering, integer NINC, forcing aggregation, and endpoint conventions can still make a one-day update differ from twenty-four hourly updates.

content.title: Close the implemented weighted balance
content.scenario: P=12 mm, ET=2 mm, TCI=5 mm, BFNCC=1 mm, pervious storage rises 5 mm over area 0.7, and ADIMC rises 1 mm over ADIMP 0.5.

steps.text: Weighted pervious change is 5 times 0.7 = 3.5 mm.
Weighted ADIMC change is 1 times 0.5 = 0.5 mm.
Accounted water is 2 + 5 + 1 + 3.5 + 0.5 = 12 mm.
Residual is 12 - 12 = 0 mm.

content.interpretation: Notice that conceptual stores overlap in bookkeeping; reproduce the source's area weighting instead of summing every raw store naively.

content.title: Balance drift scales with timestep
content.observed_behavior: Residual is small for hourly steps but grows for daily steps.
content.conditions: Identical total forcing is supplied at both resolutions.
content.candidate_causes: Rate/depth mismatch; missing daily coefficient conversion; translation changed NINC truncation; output endpoint mismatch.
content.reasoning: A physical parameter bias does not usually create machine-scale conservation drift that changes sharply with resolution. Unit conversion and numerical ordering are more direct suspects.
content.recommended_action: Log rate, depth, DT in days, NINC, every storage delta, TCI, ET, and BFNCC for a single HRU and compare step-by-step.

lessons.title: HRU arrays, independent state, and area-weighted output
lessons.summary: Trace one timestep across multiple response units and distinguish per-HRU calculations from basin aggregation.

inline.text: An indexed subarea treated as internally uniform for parameters, forcing, and SAC-SMA state. In this repository, each HRU occupies one element of every allocatable parameter, forcing, state, and diagnostic array.

A Python developer can picture a list of model-state objects; a C++ developer can picture structure-of-arrays storage. The Fortran implementation chooses the latter: modelvar%uztwc(nh), parameters%uztwm(nh), and forcing%precip(nh) refer to the same HRU index. solve_sac loops from 1 through n_hrus and calls EXSAC once per HRU.

content.title: Combine two HRUs
content.scenario: HRU areas are 3 km² and 1 km²; timestep runoff depths are 2 mm and 10 mm.

steps.text: Multiply depths by relative areas: 3 times 2 = 6 and 1 times 10 = 10.
Divide the total 16 by total area 4.
The basin-average runoff depth is 4 mm.

content.result: The small flashy HRU raises the mean but does not dominate it.
content.interpretation: Using an unweighted average would report 6 mm and overstate basin runoff by 50 percent.

content.title: Changing HRU order changes results
content.observed_behavior: The same two HRUs produce different framework output after parameter rows are swapped.
content.conditions: Standalone per-HRU files remain internally plausible.
content.candidate_causes: Forcing/parameter alignment error; BMI element-one limitation; ID parsing mismatch.
content.reasoning: Independent HRU physics should be permutation-invariant after IDs are aligned. Order dependence points to indexing or an interface that exposes only the first element.
content.recommended_action: Compare hru_id ordering in parameters, forcing filenames, and framework mapping; then inspect element-one BMI getters and setters.

lessons.title: A Fortran-to-C/C++/Python translation guide
lessons.summary: Read the implementation in familiar object, reference, array, and control-flow terms without erasing Fortran semantics.

inline.text: Modern Fortran here is object-capable. A module is closest to a C++ namespace plus implementation unit or a Python module. A derived type is closest to a class/struct. Type-bound procedures are methods. The percent operator selects a field like C++ dot or Python dot. ALLOCATABLE arrays own dynamically sized contiguous storage.

content.title: One-based indices and array order

inline.text: Translate Fortran element nh to C/C++/Python element nh-1. Multidimensional Fortran arrays are column-major, unlike the usual row-major C/C++ convention. This model mostly uses one-dimensional HRU arrays, but the rule matters at interoperability boundaries.

content.title: INTENT is an API contract

inline.text: INTENT(OUT) makes the incoming value undefined on entry; it is stronger than a comment saying output. INTENT(INOUT) means the current value is consumed and then mutated. Preserve these distinctions in constness, return types, and tests.

content.title: A direct C port differs only at intense rainfall
content.observed_behavior: Most timesteps match, but high-input timesteps select a different NINC and diverge.
content.conditions: The port replaced INT with rounding and reordered updates for readability.
content.candidate_causes: Truncation-versus-rounding; changed mutation order; float precision; missing clamps.
content.reasoning: Branch thresholds and adaptive iteration counts make apparently small semantic changes observable. For positive values, Fortran INT truncates toward zero just like a C cast, not round().
content.recommended_action: Create golden tests around threshold values, port statements in source order, and compare every store after each internal increment.

lessons.title: Why the BMI driver exists and how frameworks reach Fortran
lessons.summary: Separate science from orchestration, trace initialize/update/finalize, and understand the ISO C pointer bridge used by ngen.

inline.text: A standard set of lifecycle, time, metadata, grid, and value-access functions that makes a model controllable and inspectable by a driver or coupling framework.

The BMI driver is necessary because SAC1 is only a timestep kernel: it does not decide how configuration is loaded, when forcing is supplied, how many steps to run, how other components discover variables, or when resources are released. driver_bmi.f90 is both the standalone main program and a small executable specification of the required call order. Crucially, it invokes the same BMI methods used at the framework boundary, so standalone execution tests the adapter instead of bypassing it.

content.title: Lifecycle and responsibility

steps.text: initialize(config): parse the namelist, allocate HRU arrays, read parameters and optional restart state, and prepare standalone files where build flags allow it.
get_current_time/get_end_time/get_time_step: let the driver own loop control without reaching into private model state.
set_value: in framework mode, provide tair, precip, and pet rates before update.
update(): solve every HRU once, accumulate diagnostics, then advance the clock by dt.
get_value: copy outputs and exposed metadata to the driver/framework.
finalize(): close standalone resources and finish the lifecycle.

content.code:
status = m%initialize(namelist_file)
status = m%get_current_time(current_time)
status = m%get_end_time(end_time)
do while (current_time .le. end_time)
  status = m%update()
  status = m%get_current_time(current_time)
end do
status = m%finalize()
content.caption: The standalone BMI lifecycle

content.title: BIND(C) does not make bmi_sac a C struct

inline.text: bmi_sac contains type-bound procedures and non-interoperable internals. The source exports only register_bmi with a C ABI, allocates the real Fortran object, and passes back an opaque pointer wrapper. Keep all interpretation behind the adapter.

content.title: Status values are currently ignored by the driver

inline.text: Each call overwrites status, but the standalone loop does not branch on failure. Production C++ or Python wrappers should check every status and preserve the first actionable error.

content.title: ngen loads the library but receives only zeros
content.observed_behavior: Registration succeeds and update returns success, yet outputs never respond to forcing.
content.conditions: The model was built in framework mode.
content.candidate_causes: Forcing was not set before update; wrong variable name or units; element-one HRU mismatch; failed status ignored.
content.reasoning: NGEN_FORCING_ACTIVE disables file forcing, so the framework must set tair, precip, and pet. A successful update only means the routine returned success, not that meaningful forcing was supplied.
content.recommended_action: List input names and units, set rates in mm/s, read them back, check statuses, then inspect prcp_mm after multiplication by dt.

inline.text: The default CMake configuration always builds the standalone sac executable. If ISO_C_FORTRAN_BMI_PATH names the ngen ISO C Fortran BMI project, it also builds libsacbmi as a position-independent shared library with framework forcing and output macros. Those macros remove local file responsibilities; they do not change SAC1's hydrologic equations.

content.title: Pinned defect: update_until tests the wrong quantity

inline.text: sac_update_until rejects backward time correctly, but its loop condition compares the requested time to end_datetime rather than current time to requested time. For most requested times before the run end, that condition never changes as update advances, so the call can run indefinitely. Treat update_until as defective at this revision.

content.title: Pinned metadata discrepancies

inline.text: runInfoType computes ntimes from start_datetime minus end_datetime, yielding a negative count for forward runs. BMI parameter-unit metadata labels fractions and recession coefficients as mm. get_value converts tci from mm to m, while set_value stores a supplied tci without the inverse conversion. Tests and clients must not trust metadata blindly.

content.title: Endpoint semantics deserve a regression test

inline.text: The driver updates while current_time is less than or equal to end_time, then advances the clock inside update. That inclusive condition may execute a step beginning at the configured end timestamp. Define whether timestamps label interval starts or ends and test the expected count.

content.title: A framework hangs during partial advancement
content.observed_behavior: A call intended to advance to a timestamp before the simulation end never returns.
content.conditions: initialize succeeded and ordinary update calls work.
content.candidate_causes: sac_update_until loop defect; zero dt; corrupt end time.
content.reasoning: At the pinned source, the loop condition time < end_datetime does not depend on changing current time, so repeated updates cannot make it false.
content.recommended_action: Capture a stack trace, verify the source lines, avoid update_until, loop over checked update calls in the driver, and add a regression test before fixing the condition.
